## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to implement a core low-level primitive in a branchless, edge-case-safe way, a common requirement in bitboard games, crypto utilities, and high-performance kernels.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation semantics (wraps around word).
- Safe shifts with modulo-64 trick: ((0 - s) & 63).
- Branchless implementation for predictable performance.

## Code Example
```javascript
uint64_t rotateLeft64(uint64_t n, unsigned int k) {
  unsigned int s = k & 63;
  return (n << s) | (n >> ((0 - s) & 63));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to 128-bit words?
- What are potential portability concerns across compilers regarding shift behavior?

## Why This Is Asked

Assesses ability to manipulate a 128-bit value using two 64-bit parts and leverage available intrinsics for performance. It tests understanding of bit significance ordering and boundary cases (zero input).

## Key Concepts

- 128-bit represented as two 64-bit words (lo then hi) and how trailing zeros map across the boundary
- Using 64-bit ctz intrinsics to build a 128-bit result in constant time
- Correct handling of the all-zero input returning 128

## Code Example

```c
int trailingZeroCount128(uint128 x) {
  if (x.lo != 0) return __builtin_ctzll(x.lo);
  if (x.hi != 0) return 64 + __builtin_ctzll(x.hi);
  return 128;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you implement this without compiler intrinsics?
- How would you port the approach to a 256-bit representation?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Matters
Tests the ability to implement bitwise rotation on 128-bit words without branches, while safely handling edge cases.

## Key Concepts
- **Bitwise rotation**: Moves bits cyclically; bits shifted out one end re-enter from the other.
- **Safe shift masking**: The `k &= 127` constrains k to [0, 127], preventing undefined behavior when k >= word width.
- **No loops or conditionals**: Shift and OR operations execute in constant time for low-latency systems.

## Code Breakdown
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, unsigned int k) {
  k &= 127;                    // mask to valid range
  return (x << k) | (x >> (128 - k));  // rotate via split-shift-OR
}
```
- `(x << k)` moves the high bits toward the left, discarding overflow.
- `(x >> (128 - k))` captures the bits that "wrap around" to the right.
- OR combines both halves into a single cyclic result.

## Why This Is Asked

Tests branchless bitwise selection across a 128-bit value. It mirrors practical use cases like compositing two 128-bit values with a mask in a single pass.

## Key Concepts

- Branchless bitwise selection
- 128-bit composition via hi/lo fields
- Handling of full-range masks across both lanes

## Code Example

```c
uint128 blend128(uint128 a, uint128 b, uint128 mask) {
  uint128 t1 = and128(a, mask);
  uint128 t2 = and128(b, not128(mask));
  return or128(t1, t2);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you validate correctness across all 2^128 mask patterns efficiently?
- How would this approach extend to 256-bit operands with the same interface?
